claim: Src42A constitutively active (CA) expression induces cell proliferation in the wing imaginal disc, detected by phospho-histone 3 (pH3) staining.
source: Src42A constitutively active (CA) expression induces cell proliferation, which was detected by phospho-histone 3 (pH3) staining.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1A-B and quantified in Figure 1B, demonstrating increased pH3+ cells in Src42A CA-expressing regions.

claim: Src42A CA expression induces caspase activation in the wing imaginal disc, detected by cleaved DCP1 staining.
source: Src42A CA expression induces caspase activation, which was detected by cleaved DCP1 staining.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1C-D and quantified in Figure 1D, showing increased cDCP1+ cells in Src42A CA-expressing regions.

claim: Src42A CA expression results in mild overgrowth in the expressing region.
source: This provocation of both cell proliferation and death results in a mild overgrowth in the Src42A CA-expressing region, likely reflecting the mutually cancelling effects of proliferation and death. (Figure 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by volume quantification data shown in Figure 1E, demonstrating increased GFP+ cell volume in Src42A CA-expressing regions.

claim: Src-induced cell death cannot be inhibited by p21 overexpression, which suppresses cell proliferation.
source: It has previously been shown that Src-induced cell death cannot be inhibited by p21 overexpression, which suppresses cell proliferation (Pedraza et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work by Pedraza et al., 2004.

claim: Src42A CA expression in the wing disc induces organismal lethality.
source: The screening took advantage of the organismal lethality induced by Src42A CA expression in the wing disc (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by survival rate data shown in Figure 2A, demonstrating reduced survival in flies expressing Src42A CA.

claim: Knockdown of slpr suppresses Src42A CA-induced organismal lethality.
source: Src-induced lethality was suppressed by slpr knockdown (Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: The claim is supported by survival rate data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A-B, demonstrating improved survival when slpr is knocked down in Src42A CA-expressing flies.

claim: Rare escapers of vg>Src42A CA flies have small, disheveled wings.
source: Rare escapers of vg>Src42A CA flies have small, disheveled wings, but slpr knockdown completely reversed this phenotype (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by wing phenotype images shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: slpr knockdown completely reverses the small, disheveled wing phenotype of vg>Src42A CA escapers.
source: Rare escapers of vg>Src42A CA flies have small, disheveled wings, but slpr knockdown completely reversed this phenotype (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by wing phenotype images shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, demonstrating normal wing morphology when slpr is knocked down.

claim: Slpr inhibition in the eye disc suppresses organismal lethality induced by Src expression.
source: This is not an event that is observed only in the wing disc because Slpr inhibition in the eye disc also suppressed organismal lethality and the abnormal eye phenotype of escapers that are induced by the Src expression in the eye disc (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by survival rate data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E, demonstrating improved survival when slpr is knocked down in eye disc-specific Src42A-expressing flies.

claim: Slpr was originally identified as a JNKKK, a MAPKKK that regulates JNK signaling.
source: Slpr was originally identified as a JNKKK, a MAPKKK that regulates JNK signaling (Stronach and Perrimon, 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work by Stronach and Perrimon, 2002.

claim: Src has long been known to regulate JNK signaling.
source: Src has long been known to regulate JNK signaling (Tateno et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work by Tateno et al., 2000.

claim: slpr RNAi significantly suppresses Src-mediated activation of JNK, detected by the JNK activity reporter TRE-RFP.
source: Indeed, slpr RNAi significantly suppressed Src-mediated activation of JNK, which was detected by the JNK activity reporter TRE-RFP (Figure 2C–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by TRE-RFP reporter data shown in Figure 2C-D, demonstrating reduced JNK activity when slpr is knocked down in Src42A CA-expressing cells.

claim: Slpr is a JNKKK that transduces Src activation to JNK signaling.
source: This observation suggests that Slpr is a JNKKK that transduces Src activation to JNK signaling.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that slpr knockdown suppresses Src-mediated JNK activation, as shown in Figure 2C-D.

claim: A combination of JNK inhibition and Src activation is known to induce a massive overgrowth phenotype.
source: This is because a combination of JNK inhibition and Src activation is known to induce a massive overgrowth phenotype (Enomoto and Igaki, 2013; Ho et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work by Enomoto and Igaki, 2013 and Ho et al., 2015.

claim: Simultaneously activating Src and suppressing JNK results in substantial overgrowth of the wing disc.
source: Indeed, simultaneously activating Src and suppressing JNK resulted in substantial overgrowth of the wing disc (Figure 3A–D) and complete organismal lethality (Figure 3E).
evidence: The claim is supported by volume quantification data shown in Figure 3C and images in Figure 3A-B, demonstrating massive overgrowth when Src is activated and JNK is inhibited.

claim: Combining Src activation and Slpr inhibition does not induce tissue overgrowth.
source: On the other hand, combining Src activation and Slpr inhibition did not induce tissue overgrowth (Figure 3A–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by volume quantification data shown in Figure 3C and images in Figure 3A-B, demonstrating no overgrowth when Src is activated and slpr is knocked down.

claim: Slpr inhibition suppresses both cell proliferation and apoptosis induced by Src.
source: We found that Slpr inhibition suppressed both cell proliferation and apoptosis induced by Src whereas JNK inhibition suppressed only apoptosis but not cell proliferation (Figure 3A–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by pH3 quantification data shown in Figure 3D and cDCP1 staining shown in Figure 3A, demonstrating that slpr knockdown reduces both proliferation and apoptosis in Src42A CA-expressing cells.

claim: JNK inhibition suppresses only apoptosis but not cell proliferation induced by Src.
source: We found that Slpr inhibition suppressed both cell proliferation and apoptosis induced by Src whereas JNK inhibition suppressed only apoptosis but not cell proliferation (Figure 3A–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by pH3 quantification data shown in Figure 3D and cDCP1 staining shown in Figure 3A, demonstrating that JNK inhibition reduces apoptosis but not proliferation in Src42A CA-expressing cells.

claim: JNK inhibition-mediated suppression of apoptosis is responsible for tumor overgrowth when combined with Src activation.
source: This suggests that JNK inhibition-mediated suppression of apoptosis is responsible for the tumor overgrowth.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that JNK inhibition suppresses apoptosis but not proliferation, leading to overgrowth when combined with Src activation.

claim: A combination of Src activation and apoptosis inhibition by microRNAs for reaper, hid and grim induces overgrowth, similar to JNK inhibition.
source: Consistent with this idea, a combination of Src activation and apoptosis inhibition by microRNAs for reaper, hid and grim (Siegrist et al., 2010), which inhibits DIAP1, also induced overgrowth, similar to JNK inhibition (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by images shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E, demonstrating overgrowth when Src is activated and apoptosis is inhibited by miRNA RGH.

claim: A combination of Src activation and cell death induction enhances survival over the Src tumor.
source: On the other hand, a combination of Src activation and cell death induction enhanced survival over the Src tumor (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by survival rate data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1F, demonstrating improved survival when cell death is induced in Src42A CA-expressing flies.

claim: The overgrowth phenotype induced by Src activation and JNK inhibition is suppressed by slpr knockdown.
source: Furthermore, the overgrowth phenotype induced by Src activation and JNK inhibition was suppressed by slpr knockdown (Figure 3—figure supplement 1G–I).
evidence: The claim is supported by volume and pH3 quantification data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1H-I, demonstrating reduced overgrowth when slpr is knocked down in Src42A CA and JNK DN-expressing cells.

claim: Slpr regulates other signaling pathways along with the JNK pathway.
source: Taken together, these findings strongly imply that Slpr, which was originally identified as a MAPKKK upstream of JNK, regulates other signaling pathways along with the JNK pathway.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that slpr knockdown suppresses both proliferation and apoptosis, while JNK inhibition only suppresses apoptosis.

claim: Slpr was originally identified as a MAPKKK upstream of JNK.
source: Although Slpr was originally identified as a JNK regulator (Stronach and Perrimon, 2002), subsequent studies report the existence of situations where Slpr can also activate other MAPKs including Erk and p38 (Chen et al., 2010; Sathyanarayana et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work by Stronach and Perrimon, 2002.

claim: Subsequent studies report that Slpr can also activate other MAPKs including Erk and p38.
source: Although Slpr was originally identified as a JNK regulator (Stronach and Perrimon, 2002), subsequent studies report the existence of situations where Slpr can also activate other MAPKs including Erk and p38 (Chen et al., 2010; Sathyanarayana et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work by Chen et al., 2010 and Sathyanarayana et al., 2003.

claim: Src activates both Erk and p38 in the wing disc.
source: We found that Src activates both Erk and p38 in the wing disc (Figure 4A–B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by phospho-Erk and phospho-p38 staining data shown in Figure 4A-B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A-C, demonstrating increased phosphorylation of both MAPKs in Src42A CA-expressing cells.

claim: Activated Erk and p38 are observed not only in the region that expresses Src, but also in the surrounding area together with non-cell autonomous proliferation.
source: Activated Erk and p38 were observed not only in the region that expresses Src, but also in the surrounding area together with non-cell autonomous proliferation (Figure 4A–B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by phospho-Erk and phospho-p38 staining data shown in Figure 4A-B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A-D, demonstrating activation of these MAPKs in both GFP+ and GFP- cells.

claim: There is non-cell autonomous activation of JNK and cell death by Src, albeit much subtler than Erk and p38.
source: In fact, there was also non-cell autonomous activation of JNK and cell death, albeit much subtler than Erk and p38 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E–G).
evidence: The claim is supported by TRE-RFP and cDCP1 staining data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E-G, demonstrating non-cell autonomous JNK activation and apoptosis in GFP- cells.

claim: Inhibition of Slpr reduces Src-induced activation of both p38 and Erk cell autonomously.
source: Inhibition of Slpr reduced Src-induced activation of both p38 and Erk (Figure 4A–B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–B) cell autonomously, indicating that Slpr activates p38 and Erk in addition to JNK.
evidence: The claim is supported by phospho-p38 and phospho-Erk quantification data shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B, demonstrating reduced MAPK activation when slpr is knocked down in Src42A CA-expressing cells.

claim: Slpr activates p38 and Erk in addition to JNK.
source: Inhibition of Slpr reduced Src-induced activation of both p38 and Erk (Figure 4A–B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–B) cell autonomously, indicating that Slpr activates p38 and Erk in addition to JNK.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that slpr knockdown reduces Src-induced activation of p38 and Erk, as shown in Figure 4A-B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A-B.

claim: Slpr inhibition suppresses Src-induced non-cell autonomous activation of p38 but not Erk or JNK.
source: It is of note that Slpr inhibition suppressed Src-induced non-cell autonomous activation of p38 but not Erk or JNK (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–C,E), suggesting that there are different mechanisms that regulate non-cell autonomous activation of these MAPKs.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B, E, demonstrating that slpr knockdown suppresses non-cell autonomous p38 activation but not Erk or JNK activation.

claim: There are different mechanisms that regulate non-cell autonomous activation of p38, Erk, and JNK.
source: It is of note that Slpr inhibition suppressed Src-induced non-cell autonomous activation of p38 but not Erk or JNK (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–C,E), suggesting that there are different mechanisms that regulate non-cell autonomous activation of these MAPKs.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that slpr knockdown has differential effects on non-cell autonomous activation of different MAPKs.

claim: Slpr inhibition does not affect non-cell autonomous activation of caspase.
source: In line with persistence of the non-cell autonomous JNK activation with Slpr inhibition, Slpr inhibition did not affect non-cell autonomous activation of caspase ( Figure 4—figure supplement 1E, F, G).
evidence: The claim is supported by cDCP1 quantification data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1G, demonstrating no change in non-cell autonomous apoptosis when slpr is knocked down.

claim: Src-invoked proliferation does not occur as a compensatory proliferation induced by death of the surrounding cells.
source: This suggests that Src-invoked proliferation does not occur as a compensatory proliferation induced by death of the surrounding cells.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that slpr knockdown does not affect non-cell autonomous caspase activation, as shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E-G.

claim: Erk inhibition is unable to reverse Src-induced organismal lethality and proliferation.
source: When we inhibited Erk using several RNAis that had previously been utilized (Singh et al., 2016), Erk inhibition was unable to reverse Src-induced organismal lethality and proliferation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1H–I).
evidence: The claim is supported by survival rate data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1H and images in Figure 4—figure supplement 1I, demonstrating that erk RNAi does not suppress Src-induced lethality or proliferation.

claim: Even though Src-Slpr signaling activates Erk, its functional contribution to proliferation is negligible.
source: This indicates that, even though Src-Slpr signaling activates Erk, its functional contribution to proliferation is negligible.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that Erk inhibition does not suppress Src-induced proliferation, as shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1I.

claim: Erk inhibition lowers survival over Src expression.
source: In fact, Erk inhibition lowered survival over Src expression, implying that Src-Slpr-Erk signaling is protective for animals through an unknown mechanism.
evidence: The claim is supported by survival rate data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1H, demonstrating reduced survival when erk is knocked down in Src42A CA-expressing flies.

claim: Src-Slpr-Erk signaling is protective for animals through an unknown mechanism.
source: In fact, Erk inhibition lowered survival over Src expression, implying that Src-Slpr-Erk signaling is protective for animals through an unknown mechanism.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that Erk inhibition reduces survival in Src-expressing flies, as shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1H.

claim: p38 inhibition suppresses cell proliferation induced by Src.
source: On the other hand, when we inhibited p38 in the Src-expressing region, it suppressed cell proliferation (Figure 4C–E), regardless of the existence of JNK inhibition (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by volume and pH3 quantification data shown in Figure 4D-E, demonstrating reduced proliferation when p38 is inhibited in Src42A CA-expressing cells.

claim: Inhibition of the p38 MAPKK, Licorne (Lic), suppresses Src-induced proliferation.
source: Furthermore, inhibition of the p38 MAPKK, Licorne (Lic) (Cully et al., 2010), suppressed Src-induced proliferation (Figure 4—figure supplement 2D–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by volume and pH3 quantification data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2E-F, demonstrating reduced proliferation when lic is knocked down in Src42A CA and JNK DN-expressing cells.

claim: p38 inhibition suppresses Src-induced lethality.
source: p38 inhibition also suppressed Src-induced lethality (Figure 4F).
evidence: The claim is supported by survival rate data shown in Figure 4F, demonstrating improved survival when p38 is inhibited in Src42A CA-expressing flies.

claim: p38 suppression does not inhibit Src-mediated apoptosis.
source: Importantly, p38 suppression did not inhibit Src-mediated apoptosis (Figure 4—figure supplement 2G–I).
evidence: The claim is supported by cDCP1 quantification data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2H-I, demonstrating no change in apoptosis volume when p38 is inhibited in Src42A CA-expressing cells.

claim: Downstream of Src-Slpr, p38 regulates cell proliferation without affecting apoptosis.
source: We conclude that, downstream of Src-Slpr, p38 regulates cell proliferation without affecting apoptosis.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observations that p38 inhibition suppresses proliferation but not apoptosis in Src-expressing cells, as shown in Figure 4C-E and Figure 4—figure supplement 2G-I.

claim: p38 regulates cell proliferation through Tor.
source: We next shifted our focus to Tor signaling since p38 also regulates cell proliferation through Tor (Cully et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work by Cully et al., 2010.

claim: Tor is a central growth regulator that transduces nutritional information to cell growth.
source: Tor is a central growth regulator that transduces nutritional information to cell growth (Kim and Guan, 2019; Sabatini, 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work by Kim and Guan, 2019 and Sabatini, 2017.

claim: Phosphorylation of 4EBP is enhanced by Src expression.
source: Phosphorylation of 4EBP, a readout of Tor signaling activation, was enhanced by Src expression (Figure 5A–B).
evidence: The claim is supported by phospho-4EBP staining data shown in Figure 5A-B, demonstrating increased 4EBP phosphorylation in Src42A CA-expressing cells.

claim: Src promotes phosphorylation of S6, another readout of Tor signaling.
source: Src also promoted phosphorylation of S6, another readout of Tor signaling (Kim et al., 2017, Figure 5—figure supplement 1B–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by phospho-S6 staining data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B-C, demonstrating increased S6 phosphorylation in Src42A CA-expressing cells.

claim: Src-induced phosphorylation of 4EBP can be suppressed by Slpr or p38 inhibition, but not by JNK inhibition.
source: Src-induced phosphorylation of 4EBP and of S6 could be suppressed by Slpr or p38 inhibition, but not by JNK inhibition (Figure 5A–B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1B–C), indicating that Tor signaling functions downstream of the Src-Slpr-p38 axis.
evidence: The claim is supported by phospho-4EBP quantification data shown in Figure 5B and phospho-S6 quantification data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C, demonstrating that slpr or p38 inhibition, but not JNK inhibition, reduces Tor activation.

claim: Tor signaling functions downstream of the Src-Slpr-p38 axis.
source: Src-induced phosphorylation of 4EBP and of S6 could be suppressed by Slpr or p38 inhibition, but not by JNK inhibition (Figure 5A–B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1B–C), indicating that Tor signaling functions downstream of the Src-Slpr-p38 axis.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that Slpr or p38 inhibition suppresses Src-induced Tor activation, as shown in Figure 5A-B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B-C.

claim: Tor inhibition completely suppresses overgrowth induced by Src activation and JNK inhibition.
source: Tor inhibition completely suppressed overgrowth induced by Src activation and JNK inhibition (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is supported by images shown in Figure 5C, demonstrating no overgrowth when Tor is knocked down in Src42A CA and JNK DN-expressing cells.

claim: p38 regulates cell proliferation through Tor signaling.
source: Taken together, these findings indicate that p38 regulates cell proliferation through Tor signaling.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observations that p38 inhibition suppresses Tor activation and that Tor inhibition suppresses proliferation, as shown in Figure 5A-C.

claim: Simple dilution of yeast in the fly food suppresses tumor overgrowth induced by Src activation and JNK inhibition.
source: We found that simple dilution of yeast in the fly food suppressed the tumor overgrowth and Tor activation that are induced by Src activation and JNK inhibition (Figure 6A–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by volume quantification data shown in Figure 6C and images in Figure 6A-B, demonstrating reduced overgrowth when yeast is diluted in the diet of Src42A CA and JNK DN-expressing flies.

claim: Yeast dilution suppresses Tor activation induced by Src activation and JNK inhibition.
source: We found that simple dilution of yeast in the fly food suppressed the tumor overgrowth and Tor activation that are induced by Src activation and JNK inhibition (Figure 6A–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by phospho-4EBP quantification data shown in Figure 6D and images in Figure 6A-B, demonstrating reduced Tor activation when yeast is diluted in the diet of Src42A CA and JNK DN-expressing flies.

claim: Yeast dilution does not affect Src-induced p38 activation.
source: Yeast dilution did not affect Src-induced p38 activation (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–B), suggesting that nutrition signaling does not function upstream of p38.
evidence: The claim is supported by phospho-p38 quantification data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B, demonstrating no change in p38 activation when yeast is diluted in the diet of Src42A CA-expressing flies.

claim: Nutrition signaling does not function upstream of p38.
source: Yeast dilution did not affect Src-induced p38 activation (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–B), suggesting that nutrition signaling does not function upstream of p38.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that yeast dilution does not affect p38 activation, as shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A-B.

claim: Yeast dilution increases survival over the Src-induced stress.
source: Importantly, yeast dilution increased survival over the Src-induced stress (Figure 6E), demonstrating the connection between organismal physiology and tumorigenesis.
evidence: The claim is supported by survival rate data shown in Figure 6E, demonstrating improved survival when yeast is diluted in the diet of Src42A CA-expressing flies.

claim: Feeding of essential amino acids, but not non-essential ones, enhances lethality induced by Src expression.
source: Feeding of essential amino acids, but not non-essential ones, enhanced lethality induced by Src expression (Figure 7A).
evidence: The claim is supported by survival rate data shown in Figure 7A, demonstrating reduced survival when essential amino acids are added to the diet of Src42A CA-expressing flies.

claim: Only methionine subtraction from the diet reverses lethality of Src-activated flies induced by feeding essential amino acids.
source: Out of all the essential amino acids, only methionine subtraction reversed lethality of the Src-activated flies induced by feeding essential amino acids (Figure 7B).
evidence: The claim is supported by survival rate data shown in Figure 7B, demonstrating improved survival when methionine is subtracted from the essential amino acid mixture in the diet of Src42A CA-expressing flies.

claim: Methionine addition reduces the survival over the Src-induced stress.
source: We found that methionine addition reduces the survival over the Src-induced stress (Figure 7C), whereas it does not affect survival of control animals (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by survival rate data shown in Figure 7C, demonstrating reduced survival when methionine is added to the diet of Src42A CA-expressing flies.

claim: Methionine addition does not affect survival of control animals.
source: We found that methionine addition reduces the survival over the Src-induced stress (Figure 7C), whereas it does not affect survival of control animals (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by survival rate data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A, demonstrating no change in survival when methionine is added to the diet of control flies.

claim: Expression of Src42A CA in the wing disc decreases the circulating methionine in the hemolymph.
source: This metabolomics analysis revealed that the methionine concentration in the hemolymph is significantly decreased in flies that bear Src-induced tumors compared to control flies (Figure 7D and Figure 7—figure supplement 1C–D), which is correlated with the effects of dietary manipulation of methionine.
evidence: The claim is supported by LC-MS/MS data shown in Figure 7D, demonstrating reduced methionine concentration in the hemolymph of Src42A CA-expressing flies.

claim: Feeding methionine enhances Src-induced Tor signaling and overgrowth.
source: Feeding methionine enhanced Src-induced Tor signaling and overgrowth (Figure 7E–H), indicating that methionine is at least partly responsible for the nutrition-mediated activation of Tor signaling in Src-mediated tumors.
evidence: The claim is supported by volume and phospho-4EBP quantification data shown in Figure 7G-H, demonstrating increased overgrowth and Tor activation when methionine is added to the diet of Src42A CA and JNK DN-expressing flies.

claim: Methionine is at least partly responsible for the nutrition-mediated activation of Tor signaling in Src-mediated tumors.
source: Feeding methionine enhanced Src-induced Tor signaling and overgrowth (Figure 7E–H), indicating that methionine is at least partly responsible for the nutrition-mediated activation of Tor signaling in Src-mediated tumors.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that methionine feeding enhances Tor activation in Src tumors, as shown in Figure 7E-H.

claim: Methionine addition does not affect Src-induced caspase activation.
source: Methionine addition did not affect Src-induced caspase activation (Figure 7—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by cDCP1 staining data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2A, demonstrating no change in apoptosis when methionine is added to the diet of Src42A CA-expressing flies.

claim: Requirement of methionine for cell proliferation is relatively specific to tumor growth.
source: Requirement of methionine for cell proliferation was relatively specific to tumor growth, because, under a normal condition without tumor, addition of methionine could not reverse the effects of yeast dilution, which induces smaller adult wings in control (Figure 7—figure supplement 2B–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by wing size quantification data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2B-C, demonstrating that methionine addition does not rescue the wing size defects caused by yeast dilution in control flies.

claim: Methionine can activate Tor through its conversion to SAM, a universal methyl donor.
source: Methionine can activate Tor through its conversion to SAM, a universal methyl donor (Gu et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work by Gu et al., 2017.

claim: Inhibition of Sam synthetase suppresses both Src-induced overgrowth and Tor activation.
source: Consistently, inhibition of Sam synthetase, which converts methionine to SAM (Obata and Miura, 2015), suppressed both Src-induced overgrowth and Tor activation (Figure 7I–K).
evidence: The claim is supported by volume and phospho-4EBP quantification data shown in Figure 7J-K, demonstrating reduced overgrowth and Tor activation when SamS is knocked down in Src42A CA and JNK DN-expressing cells.

claim: Methionine regulates Tor signaling in Src tumors in a tissue-autonomous manner.
source: This indicates that methionine regulates Tor signaling in Src tumors in a tissue-autonomous manner.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that Sam synthetase inhibition suppresses Tor activation in Src tumors, as shown in Figure 7I-K.

claim: Samtor is a recently identified SAM sensor that inhibits Tor, which is released by SAM, in both mammals and Drosophila.
source: Samtor is a recently identified SAM sensor that inhibits Tor, which is released by SAM, in both mammals and Drosophila (Gu et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work by Gu et al., 2017.

claim: In a diluted yeast condition, samtor knockdown enhances Tor activation with Src.
source: As expected, in a diluted yeast condition, which suppresses Tor activation, samtor knockdown enhanced Tor activation with Src (Figure 7—figure supplement 2D–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by phospho-S6 quantification data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2F, demonstrating increased Tor activation when samtor is knocked down in Src42A CA and JNK DN-expressing cells on diluted yeast diet.

claim: samtor knockdown suppresses Src-mediated overgrowth in spite of its Tor activation.
source: Unexpectedly, however, samtor knockdown suppressed Src-mediated overgrowth in spite of its Tor activation.
evidence: The claim is supported by volume quantification data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2E, demonstrating reduced overgrowth when samtor is knocked down in Src42A CA and JNK DN-expressing cells on diluted yeast diet.

claim: Src tumors uptake more methionine than control.
source: Consistent with this idea, Src tumors uptake more methionine than control, which was demonstrated by performing an in vitro culture of the wing disc with a methionine analog homopropargylglycine (HPG) (Figure 8A–B).
evidence: The claim is supported by HPG incorporation assay data shown in Figure 8A-B, demonstrating increased HPG intensity in Src42A CA and JNK DN-expressing wing discs.

claim: Src tumors exhibit a higher ratio of SAM to methionine.
source: Furthermore, Src tumors exhibit a higher ratio of SAM to methionine (Figure 8C), indicating enhanced methionine flux to SAM.
evidence: The claim is supported by LC-MS data shown in Figure 8C, demonstrating increased SAM/methionine ratio in Src42A CA and JNK DN-expressing wing discs.

claim: Src enhances methionine uptake and methionine flux.
source: Collectively, Src enhances methionine uptake and methionine flux.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observations that Src tumors uptake more methionine and have a higher SAM/methionine ratio, as shown in Figure 8A-C.

claim: Src-mediated control of methionine metabolism is independent of p38.
source: Interestingly, this Src-mediated control of methionine metabolism was independent of p38 (Figure 8D–F, Figure 8—figure supplement 1A), suggesting that Src does activate methionine metabolism but not through p38.
evidence: The claim is supported by HPG incorporation and methionine flux data shown in Figure 8D-F and Figure 8—figure supplement 1A, demonstrating that p38 inhibition does not affect methionine uptake or flux in Src tumors.

claim: Src activates methionine metabolism but not through p38.
source: Interestingly, this Src-mediated control of methionine metabolism was independent of p38 (Figure 8D–F, Figure 8—figure supplement 1A), suggesting that Src does activate methionine metabolism but not through p38.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that p38 inhibition does not affect Src-mediated methionine metabolism, as shown in Figure 8D-F and Figure 8—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Src, the first identified oncogene, simultaneously drives cell proliferation and death in an obligatorily coupled manner through parallel MAPK pathways.
source: Here, we reveal that Src, the first identified oncogene, simultaneously drives cell proliferation and death in an obligatorily coupled manner through parallel MAPK pathways.
evidence: The claim is supported by the data presented throughout the manuscript showing that Src activates both JNK (leading to apoptosis) and p38 (leading to proliferation) through Slpr.

claim: The two MAPK pathways diverge from a lynchpin protein Slpr.
source: The two MAPK pathways diverge from a lynchpin protein Slpr.
evidence: The claim is supported by the data showing that Slpr mediates both JNK and p38 activation downstream of Src, as shown in Figures 2-4.

claim: A MAPK p38 drives proliferation whereas another MAPK JNK drives apoptosis independently of proliferation signals.
source: A MAPK p38 drives proliferation whereas another MAPK JNK drives apoptosis independently of proliferation signals.
evidence: The claim is supported by the data showing that p38 inhibition suppresses proliferation but not apoptosis, while JNK inhibition suppresses apoptosis but not proliferation, as shown in Figures 3-4.

claim: Src-p38-induced proliferation is regulated by methionine-mediated Tor signaling.
source: Src-p38-induced proliferation is regulated by methionine-mediated Tor signaling.
evidence: The claim is supported by the data showing that p38 activates Tor signaling and that methionine regulates Tor activation in Src tumors, as shown in Figures 5-7.

claim: Reduction of dietary methionine uncouples the obligatory coupling of cell proliferation and death, suppressing tumorigenesis and tumor-induced lethality.
source: Reduction of dietary methionine uncouples the obligatory coupling of cell proliferation and death, suppressing tumorigenesis and tumor-induced lethality.
evidence: The claim is supported by the data showing that methionine restriction improves survival and reduces tumor growth in Src-expressing flies, as shown in Figures 6-7.

claim: Tumorigenesis requires activation and inactivation of not one, but multiple signaling pathways.
source: Tumorigenesis requires activation and inactivation of not one, but multiple signaling pathways (Hanahan and Weinberg, 2011; Lowe et al., 2004; Shortt and Johnstone, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work by Hanahan and Weinberg, 2011; Lowe et al., 2004; and Shortt and Johnstone, 2012.

claim: Cells have evolutionarily refined fail-safe mechanisms to prevent tumorigenesis by a single oncogene activation.
source: This is likely because cells have evolutionarily refined fail-safe mechanisms to prevent tumorigenesis by a single oncogene activation.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about tumor suppressor mechanisms.

claim: The transforming effects of oncogenes are often cancelled by the cell's intrinsic ability to prevent tumorigenesis.
source: Because of this fail-safe mechanism, the transforming effects of oncogenes are often cancelled by the cell's intrinsic ability to prevent tumorigenesis (Lowe et al., 2004; Shortt and Johnstone, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work by Lowe et al., 2004 and Shortt and Johnstone, 2012.

claim: Myc is a potent oncogene implicated in most human tumor entities.
source: Myc is a potent oncogene implicated in most human tumor entities, but it is also a powerful cell death driver (Evan et al., 1992; Hoffman and Liebermann, 1998; Prendergast, 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work by Evan et al., 1992; Hoffman and Liebermann, 1998; and Prendergast, 1999.

claim: Myc is a powerful cell death driver.
source: Myc is a potent oncogene implicated in most human tumor entities, but it is also a powerful cell death driver (Evan et al., 1992; Hoffman and Liebermann, 1998; Prendergast, 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work by Evan et al., 1992; Hoffman and Liebermann, 1998; and Prendergast, 1999.

claim: Myc drives p53-mediated apoptosis through transcriptional regulation of the tumor suppressor ARF.
source: Although these two models are not mutually exclusive, delineation of Myc signaling supports the dual model: Myc drives p53-mediated apoptosis through transcriptional regulation of the tumor suppressor ARF (Lowe et al., 2004; Shortt and Johnstone, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work by Lowe et al., 2004 and Shortt and Johnstone, 2012.

claim: Many oncogenes are known to induce cell death.
source: In addition to Myc, many other oncogenes are known to induce cell death.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about oncogene-induced cell death.

claim: Oncogene-induced cell death is now accepted as an intrinsic tumor suppressive mechanism.
source: This phenomenon is now accepted as an intrinsic tumor suppressive mechanism (Shortt and Johnstone, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work by Shortt and Johnstone, 2012.

claim: How other oncogenes, such as Ras or Src, couple cell proliferation and death remains unclear.
source: However, contrary to the well-studied mechanisms of Myc-induced cell death, how other oncogenes, such as Ras or Src, couple cell proliferation and death remains unclear (Lowe et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work by Lowe et al., 2004.

claim: Src is the first oncogene identified.
source: Src is the first oncogene identified (Yeatman, 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work by Yeatman, 2004.

claim: Src expression and activity is often increased in human cancer, which contributes to oncogenesis.
source: Src expression and activity is often increased in human cancer, which contributes to oncogenesis (Ishizawar and Parsons, 2004; Summy and Gallick, 2003; Yeatman, 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work by Ishizawar and Parsons, 2004; Summy and Gallick, 2003; and Yeatman, 2004.

claim: Many clinical inhibitors targeting Src family kinases (SFKs) have been developed but their use as therapeutic drugs has been unsuccessful.
source: Due to the implication of Src in tumorigenesis, many clinical inhibitors targeting Src family kinases (SFKs) have been developed but their use as therapeutic drugs has been unsuccessful (Gargalionis et al., 2014; Sousa-Victor and Jasper, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work by Gargalionis et al., 2014 and Sousa-Victor and Jasper, 2014.

claim: Drosophila has two SFKs: Src42A and Src64B.
source: Drosophila has two SFKs: Src42A and Src64B (Kussick et al., 1993; Pedraza et al., 2004; Takahashi et al., 1996).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work by Kussick et al., 1993; Pedraza et al., 2004; and Takahashi et al., 1996.

claim: The endogenous expression patterns of Src42A and Src64B are different, but ectopic expression of either of them induces similar effects.
source: The endogenous expression patterns of Src42A and Src64B are different, but ectopic expression of either of them induces similar effects.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about Drosophila Src family kinases.

claim: Drosophila Src regulates a variety of signaling pathways, including Notch, MAPKs, Jak-Stat, EGF, Wnt, and Hippo signaling.
source: Drosophila Src regulates a variety of signaling pathways, including Notch, MAPKs, Jak-Stat, EGF, Wnt, and Hippo signaling (Cordero et al., 2014; Enomoto and Igaki, 2013; Ho et al., 2015; Read et al., 2004; Tateno et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work by Cordero et al., 2014; Enomoto and Igaki, 2013; Ho et al., 2015; Read et al., 2004; and Tateno et al., 2000.

claim: Src activation induces apoptosis as well as tissue growth.
source: Src activation induces apoptosis as well as tissue growth (Pedraza et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work by Pedraza et al., 2004.

claim: Slpr inhibition suppresses the phenotype of CA Ras overexpression.
source: Interestingly, we also found that Slpr inhibition suppresses the phenotype of CA Ras overexpression (Figure 8—figure supplement 1C, D), which, similar to Src, simultaneously induces apoptosis and proliferation (Karim and Rubin, 1998).
evidence: The claim is supported by wing phenotype and survival rate data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1C-D, demonstrating that slpr knockdown suppresses RasV12-induced phenotypes.

claim: RasV12, similar to Src, simultaneously induces apoptosis and proliferation.
source: Interestingly, we also found that Slpr inhibition suppresses the phenotype of CA Ras overexpression (Figure 8—figure supplement 1C, D), which, similar to Src, simultaneously induces apoptosis and proliferation (Karim and Rubin, 1998).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work by Karim and Rubin, 1998.

claim: Slpr could function as a lynchpin hub that integrates inputs from multiple oncogenes.
source: This suggests that Slpr could function as a lynchpin hub that integrates inputs from multiple oncogenes.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that Slpr mediates signaling from both Src and Ras, as shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1C-D.

claim: Among the amino acid transporters and GATOR complex components examined, only pathetic (path) was significantly induced by Src in a p38-dependent manner.
source: We found that among the amino acid transporters and GATOR complex components examined, only pathetic (path), an SLC36 amino acid transporter that can transport multiple amino acids, was significantly induced by Src in a p38-dependent manner (Figure 8—figure supplement 1E, F).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1E, demonstrating that path expression is increased by Src in a p38-dependent manner.

claim: Path can mediate amino acids-mediated Tor activation.
source: Since Path can mediate amino acids-mediated Tor activation (Goberdhan et al., 2005; Newton et al., 2020), we speculate that Src-p38 could regulate Tor potentially through Path-mediated uptake of non-methionine amino acids.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work by Goberdhan et al., 2005 and Newton et al., 2020.

claim: Src-p38 could regulate Tor potentially through Path-mediated uptake of non-methionine amino acids.
source: Since Path can mediate amino acids-mediated Tor activation (Goberdhan et al., 2005; Newton et al., 2020), we speculate that Src-p38 could regulate Tor potentially through Path-mediated uptake of non-methionine amino acids.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on the observation that path expression is induced by Src in a p38-dependent manner and the known function of Path in Tor activation.

claim: Nutritional state and tumorigenesis are closely linked.
source: Furthermore, our data imply that nutritional state and tumorigenesis are closely linked.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the data showing that dietary manipulation of yeast and methionine affects Src-induced tumorigenesis, as shown in Figures 6-7.

claim: In case of tumors with a high SFK activity, manipulation of dietary methionine may have a clinical benefit.
source: We speculate that, in case of tumors with a high SFK activity, manipulation of dietary methionine may have a clinical benefit.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on the findings that methionine restriction improves survival in Src-expressing flies.
